opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it starts with an observation about where the field is right now. In remote sensing, we've seen an explosion of foundation models over the last few years. Every group, every agency, every company seems to be training its own one, on Sentinel-2, on SAR, on hyperspectral, at different resolutions, with different pretraining objectives. And each of these runs costs a lot of compute, a lot of energy, and a lot of carefully curated data. At some point you have to ask yourself: are we really learning something fundamentally new with model number fifty, or are we mostly re-learning the same representations of the Earth over and over again?

That's where weight space learning comes in for us. The idea is to treat the trained neural networks themselves as a data modality. Instead of only looking at images, you look at the weights of thousands of models that have already been trained, and you ask what structure exists in that population. It turns out there's a lot of structure. You can learn representations of models, you can predict properties like accuracy or generalization just from the weights, and, more interestingly, you can generate new weights for new tasks without going through a full training run from scratch.

So for remote sensing, the vision is something like a model zoo that you can learn from. We already have this huge collection of trained models out there. If we can learn a generative model over that weight space, then when a new task comes along, say a new region, a new sensor, a new land-cover class, we can sample or initialize a good model directly, conditioned on what we know, and then fine-tune lightly. That's much cheaper than pretraining yet another foundation model.

There's also a sustainability argument that I care about a lot. Earth observation is often motivated by climate and environmental monitoring. It's a bit ironic if the way we do that is by burning enormous amounts of compute on redundant pretraining. Reusing the knowledge that's already encoded in existing weights feels like the more responsible path.

And finally, there's a scientific curiosity aspect. Weights are, in a sense, a compressed description of what a model learned about the data. If you can analyze and compare them directly, you get a new lens on questions like: what's actually different between a model trained on Europe versus Africa, or on optical versus radar? That's hard to see from the outputs alone, but it might be visible in weight space.

So I wouldn't say we should stop building foundation models entirely, but I think weight space learning is a very complementary direction, one that tries to get more out of the models we've already paid for.

r001.rationale: It proposes learning a generative model over the weights of existing remote sensing models, treating them as a shared source of reusable knowledge.

r002.rationale: It does not say that fine-tuning leaves practitioners bound to the large foundation model; it instead mentions lightly fine-tuning newly generated or initialized models.

r003.rationale: It describes conditioning on task information such as region or sensor, but not on a desired model architecture.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, thanks for having me, Sam. So let me start with the observation that got us thinking about this. In remote sensing right now we're seeing what I'd almost call a foundation model arms race. Every few months there's a new one — Prithvi, SatMAE, Clay, DOFA, Scale-MAE, you name it — each trained on a slightly different mix of Sentinel-2, Landsat, maybe some SAR, maybe some hyperspectral. And they're all good. But every one of them is a massive compute investment, and when the next one comes along, the previous one is essentially discarded. Not just the model, but the whole ecosystem around it — all the people who fine-tuned it for crop classification in Kenya, or flood mapping in Bangladesh, or whatever their downstream task was.

So the question we asked was: are those thousands of fine-tuned models actually waste? Or are they themselves a form of data? And that's really the heart of weight space learning. Instead of treating a trained neural network as a black box that you only ever run inference with, you treat the weights themselves as the object of study. A population of trained models becomes a dataset, and you learn representations over that dataset.

Why is that useful for remote sensing specifically? A few reasons. First, the domain is incredibly heterogeneous — different sensors, different resolutions, different spectral bands, different geographies, different seasons. No single foundation model, no matter how big, is going to perfectly cover all of that. But collectively, the models that practitioners train and fine-tune do span that diversity. If you can learn the structure of that weight space — what makes a model good at Arctic sea ice versus one that's good at urban land cover — you can start doing things like predicting the properties of a model without running it, or generating weights for a new sensor or region by sampling from that learned distribution, or doing zero-shot or few-shot model adaptation by moving in weight space rather than retraining from scratch.

Second, and this is maybe the more pragmatic argument, the compute economics are completely different. Training another foundation model is hundreds or thousands of GPU-days, and most groups doing applied remote sensing — agencies, NGOs, university labs — simply can't do that. But they can train small models. And if there's a shared infrastructure that can ingest those small models, learn from the population, and give back better initializations or transferred capabilities, that's a much more democratic path forward than hoping the next big lab releases something that happens to fit your needs.

And third, there's a sustainability angle that I think matters a lot in this field in particular. We're a community that spends its time studying climate, deforestation, land degradation — and then we burn enormous amounts of energy retraining models that largely relearn what the last one already knew. Weight space learning is a way of saying: the knowledge is already there, encoded in the weights of models that already exist. Let's learn to reuse it rather than rediscover it.

Now, I want to be honest that it's still early. The weight space is high-dimensional, it has these annoying symmetries — permutations of neurons, scaling invariances — that make it hard to compare two models naively, and the datasets of trained models we have so far are small compared to what we'd want. So I'm not saying stop training foundation models. I'm saying we should stop treating each one as disposable, and start treating the growing population of models as the resource it actually is.

r001.rationale: The response treats existing trained models as a dataset and says to learn representations over that population, capturing their knowledge in a learned weight-space representation.

r002.rationale: It discusses the high compute cost of training foundation models and the ability to train small models, but does not say fine-tuning leaves practitioners bound to the large model's size.

r003.rationale: It proposes sampling weights for a new sensor or region, but does not describe conditioning sampling on a desired architecture.

astra-6.text:
Well, training a foundation model for remote sensing is a substantial investment, and we already have many models that have been trained on different sensors, different regions, and different tasks. Usually, we treat each of those models as an endpoint. But its weights contain information about what it learned. So the question is: can we use those existing models themselves as data?

That’s the idea behind weight space learning. Instead of learning only from satellite images, we learn across the parameters of trained neural networks. If we can understand that space, we can potentially predict which models will transfer well to a new task, or generate useful initializations without starting every training run from scratch.

I wouldn’t say it replaces foundation models. It’s a complementary way to reuse the computation and knowledge we’ve already invested in. And remote sensing is an interesting setting because the data and tasks are so heterogeneous. The challenge is to turn that collection of specialized models into something we can learn from collectively.

r001.rationale: The response proposes learning across trained models’ parameters, but does not clearly say to compress their knowledge into a shared weight-space representation.

r002.rationale: It mentions the investment in training foundation models, but does not identify that fine-tuning leaves practitioners bound to a model’s large size.

r003.rationale: It discusses predicting transfer or generating initializations, but does not describe conditioning weight-space sampling on a desired architecture to generate its parameters.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, if you look at remote sensing, we already have a lot of trained models. They capture different sensors, different geographic regions, different seasons, and different tasks. Training another foundation model is expensive, and it doesn’t necessarily answer the question of how we can make use of all the knowledge that’s already there.

Weight space learning changes the object we learn from. Instead of learning only from satellite images, we learn from the parameters of models that have already been trained on those images. Can we identify which models contain useful knowledge for a new task? Can we predict how well they’ll transfer, or combine what they’ve learned without starting from scratch?

There are challenges, because two networks can represent very similar functions with very different weights. So you need methods that respect those symmetries. But the opportunity is to treat existing models as a resource for learning. I see that as complementary to foundation models: let’s also investigate how much we can gain from the models we already have.

r001.rationale: The response proposes learning from and combining parameters of existing models, but does not say to compress their knowledge into a shared weight-space representation.

r002.rationale: It says training another foundation model is expensive, but does not identify that fine-tuning leaves practitioners bound to the large model.

r003.rationale: It does not describe conditioning weight-space sampling on a desired architecture to generate that architecture’s parameters.
